intro: Kanakadhara Stotram is a Sanskrit hymn of praise addressed to Lakshmi, the goddess of prosperity and well-being, and it is attributed in tradition to Adi Shankara, the 8th-century philosopher-teacher. The name itself means 'stream of gold', and the text is built around a sequence of verses that describe Lakshmi's form, her glance, and her closeness to Vishnu, ending in a plea for her gracious attention. Unlike a narrative text, Kanakadhara Stotram does not tell a story within its verses; it is pure stuti, praise poetry, moving from one image of the goddess to another. It is counted among the shorter and more widely recited Lakshmi stotras in households across India, often alongside the Lakshmi Ashtakam or Sri Suktam, and is associated in popular memory with a specific episode from Shankara's life that gave the hymn its name.

groups.heading: Invocation to the goddess beside Hari
groups.body: The opening verse of Kanakadhara Stotram sets the scene at Vishnu's side, comparing the goddess's presence there to a female bee clinging to a tamala tree in bloom. The image is one of closeness and belonging rather than distance - she is described as having taken on every form of abundance that exists, and the verse asks that her playful, sidelong glance bring auspiciousness. This establishes the tone for the whole hymn: Lakshmi is approached not as a remote power but as one whose attention, even in passing, is what the devotee seeks.

groups.heading: The shy, flickering glance of Lakshmi
groups.body: The second verse turns to the goddess's eyes, describing them as moving back and forth across Vishnu's face the way a bee moves over a large lotus, held back by a mixture of affection and bashfulness. This is a verse about restraint and devotion shown through a glance rather than through words. The verse asks that this same wandering, affectionate gaze - here called the gaze of one born of the ocean, a common epithet for Lakshmi - extend prosperity to the one reciting Kanakadhara Stotram.

groups.heading: Vishnu's joy in her nearness
groups.body: Here the hymn describes Mukunda, a name for Vishnu, with eyes half-closed in quiet bliss, absorbed and unmoving, in the presence of the goddess whose pupils are described as slightly turned and lidded with pleasure. The verse is less about Lakshmi acting and more about the mood of contentment her nearness creates. The one reciting the verse asks that this same contented, overflowing state be granted to them, through her who is described as the consort of the one who reclines on the serpent.

groups.heading: A necklace of sapphire glances
groups.body: This verse compares the goddess's chain of glances toward Vishnu, resting near the Kaustubha jewel on his chest, to a garland of sapphires. It is an image of adornment and intimacy - her attention is pictured almost as jewellery worn close to the heart. The verse notes that this same gaze is capable of granting desires even to the divine, and asks that the one belonging to the lotus-seat, another name for Lakshmi, bring well-being through it.

groups.heading: Lightning against a monsoon cloud
groups.body: One of the most visual verses in Kanakadhara Stotram compares Lakshmi, shining against Vishnu's dark, cloud-like chest, to a streak of lightning flashing against a rain cloud. Vishnu is referred to here as the enemy of the demon Kaitabha, and the goddess as the revered form that is mother to all the worlds, daughter of Bhrigu. The verse asks for auspicious things through this radiant, luminous form, continuing the hymn's pattern of describing the goddess through natural imagery before making a request.

groups.heading: The glance that once favoured Indra
groups.body: This verse recalls that the position Indra holds as king of the gods was attained through the favour of this same goddess, and asks that even a fraction of her slow, half-lowered glance - described as gentle and unhurried - fall upon the one reciting. It names Vishnu as the slayer of Madhu and the goddess as daughter of the ocean. The verse is notable for asking for only a small share of her attention, continuing the hymn's humility in its requests.

groups.heading: A glance that lifts the ordinary
groups.body: The following verses describe how even those of limited or ordinary disposition can, through her compassionate glance, come easily to a state the verse compares to reaching heaven. The goddess's gaze is likened to the glow inside a lotus, full and joyful, and is asked to nurture well-being for the one reciting Kanakadhara Stotram, addressing her here as the one seated on the lotus throne.

groups.heading: The plea for the humble household
groups.body: This is the verse most often connected with the story behind Kanakadhara Stotram. It asks that a breeze of compassion bring a stream of wealth to a helpless, sorrowing young bird - a metaphor for a struggling household - and that misfortune arising from past wrongs be set at a distance, for a long time. The goddess is described through the image of a rain-cloud of eyes, moist with affection for Vishnu. Tradition holds this verse as the one directly tied to the episode that gave the hymn its title, 'stream of gold'.

groups.heading: Many names, one goddess
groups.body: The closing verse of Kanakadhara Stotram gathers several of Lakshmi's names and forms together - as the goddess of speech, as the beautiful consort of the one whose banner bears Garuda, as Shakambhari who nourishes with vegetation, as the beloved of the moon-crested Shiva - and bows to her as the eternal youthful one present through creation, preservation and dissolution. It functions as a final salutation, drawing together the different aspects praised through the earlier verses into a single gesture of reverence.

recitation: Kanakadhara Stotram is commonly recited on Fridays, a day traditionally associated with Lakshmi worship, and especially during Diwali, Varalakshmi Vratam, and other occasions dedicated to the goddess. Many households recite it as part of the morning or evening puja, after lighting a lamp before an image of Lakshmi, sometimes with fresh flowers, particularly lotus if available, and akshata (unbroken rice) offered verse by verse. It is often chanted a set number of times - repetitions of 11 or 108 are commonly mentioned in household practice - though a single complete recitation is also considered proper on an ordinary day. Some families recite it specifically when beginning a new venture, moving into a new home, or at the start of the financial year, treating the occasion as a time to seek the goddess's attention rather than as a fixed ritual obligation. It is also recited by individuals privately, without any accompanying ritual, simply as part of a regular habit of prayer. As with most stotras, pronunciation and tone are considered important by those who teach it, and it is commonly learned by listening and repeating before being recited independently, often guided by a family elder, priest, or teacher.
tradition: The tradition around Kanakadhara Stotram is closely tied to a well-known account of its composition. It is said that Adi Shankara, during his wanderings, was given an ordinary amalaka (gooseberry) fruit in alms by a poor woman who had nothing else to offer, and that moved by her situation and devotion, he composed this hymn in praise of Lakshmi on the spot. According to the account, golden amalakas are said to have showered down in response - giving the hymn its name, kanaka-dhara, 'stream of gold'. This background is why the text is traditionally associated with prosperity and relief from want, though it is recited more broadly simply as an expression of reverence toward Lakshmi. The tradition holds that reciting it is an act of devotion and request made with humility, not a transaction with a fixed result, and teachers of the text are generally careful to frame it this way - as prayer offered to the goddess's compassion, the outcome of which rests with her.

faq.a: It is traditionally attributed to Adi Shankara, the 8th-century philosopher and teacher, and is widely associated with the story of a poor woman's offering that is said to have moved him to compose it in praise of Lakshmi.

faq.q: What does the name Kanakadhara Stotram mean?
faq.a: Kanaka means gold and dhara means stream or shower, so the name translates roughly to 'stream of gold'. The name comes from the traditional account connected with the hymn's composition, in which golden fruit is said to have rained down.

faq.q: On which day should Kanakadhara Stotram be recited?
faq.a: Friday is commonly considered favourable since it is associated with Lakshmi in many households, and the hymn is also recited during Diwali and other Lakshmi-related occasions. That said, it is recited on ordinary days too, as part of regular prayer, without being limited to a particular day.

faq.q: How many times should it be recited?
faq.a: There is no single fixed rule. Many people recite it once a day, while others follow counts such as 11 or 108 repetitions, particularly during festivals. The tradition generally treats the number as a matter of personal or family practice rather than a strict requirement.

faq.q: Is Kanakadhara Stotram only about wealth?
faq.a: Not entirely. While one verse is closely tied to a plea for relief from poverty, most of Kanakadhara Stotram describes Lakshmi's form, her glance, and her closeness to Vishnu through poetic imagery, with the request for well-being woven through rather than being its sole subject.
